questions.title: Purpose of a flowchart
questions.text: Explain why a designer draws flowcharts of the processes in a new system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): shows the steps / order of a process clearly; shows decisions and loops; programmers can code from it; errors in the logic can be found before coding; easy to discuss with the client / team
scheme.model_answer: It shows the steps and decisions of each process in order, so programmers can code it correctly and logic errors are found before coding begins.

questions.title: Decision exits
questions.text: A decision symbol in a flowchart must have exactly two labelled exits.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: Which symbol
questions.text: Which symbol should be used for the step `OUTPUT "Password accepted"`?

scheme.mark_scheme: C

prefill: The condition is tested before each repetition; may run zero times
The body always runs at least once

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Count-controlled (1); 2 Pre-condition (1); 3 Post-condition (1)

questions.title: Counting and totalling
questions.text: Explain the difference between **counting** and **totalling** in a flowchart, with an example of each.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Counting adds 1 each time an event happens, e.g. count ← count + 1 (1)
- Totalling adds a value each time, e.g. total ← total + price (1)
scheme.model_answer: Counting adds 1 each time something happens (count ← count + 1); totalling adds the value itself (total ← total + price).

questions.title: Trace a flowchart
questions.text:
A flowchart does the following:

```text
total ← 0, count ← 0
repeat 4 times:
    INPUT mark
    IF mark >= 50 THEN count ← count + 1
    total ← total + mark
OUTPUT count, total
```

Complete the trace table for the marks **45, 70, 50, 30**.

questions.title: Find the error
questions.text: In a flowchart that should count the late students, the box `count ← 0` is placed **inside** the loop, just after `INPUT time`. Explain the effect of this error and how to correct it.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The count is reset to 0 on every repetition, so the final count is 0 or 1 / wrong (1)
- count ← 0 must be placed before the loop (1)
scheme.model_answer: The count is reset to 0 for every student, so at the end it can only be 0 or 1. The box count ← 0 must be moved before the start of the loop.

questions.title: Flowchart to pseudocode
questions.text: A flowchart inputs a number of tickets. If more than 2 tickets are bought, each ticket after the second has a 10% discount (a ticket costs 2000). Write the pseudocode for this flowchart, outputting the total cost.

scheme.mark_scheme:
INPUT tickets (1)
IF tickets > 2 THEN (1)
  cost ← 2 * 2000 + (tickets − 2) * 2000 * 0.9 (1)
ELSE cost ← tickets * 2000
ENDIF
OUTPUT cost (1)
scheme.model_answer:
INPUT tickets
IF tickets > 2 THEN
    cost ← 2 * 2000 + (tickets - 2) * 2000 * 0.9
ELSE
    cost ← tickets * 2000
ENDIF
OUTPUT cost

scheme.model_answer: START → INPUT a, b → a > b? Yes → OUTPUT a; No → OUTPUT b → END

questions.title: Draw: a validation loop
questions.text: Draw a flowchart that keeps asking the user for an age until a value from 11 to 18 is entered, then outputs "Accepted".

scheme.mark_scheme: INPUT age (1); decision age >= 11 AND age <= 18 (1); No → error message and loop back to input (1); Yes → OUTPUT Accepted → END (1)
scheme.model_answer: START → INPUT age → 11 ≤ age ≤ 18? No → OUTPUT Invalid → back to INPUT; Yes → OUTPUT Accepted → END

questions.title: Late arrivals
questions.text: The school has 850 students. The first lesson starts at 8:30 am. The arrival time of every student is recorded.

parts.title: Draw
parts.text: Create a flowchart for counting late students.

scheme.mark_scheme: Loop for 850 students (1); input / read each time (1); decision time > 8:30 (1); count ← count + 1 and output count after the loop (1)
scheme.model_answer: i ← 1 → i <= 850? → INPUT time[i] → time[i] > 8:30? Yes → count ← count + 1 → i ← i + 1 → back; after loop OUTPUT count

parts.title: Loop type
parts.text: State the most suitable type of loop for this process and explain why.

scheme.mark_scheme: Count-controlled / FOR loop (1); the number of repetitions (850) is known in advance (1)
scheme.model_answer: A count-controlled (FOR) loop, because it is known that exactly 850 students must be checked.

questions.title: Flowchart basics
questions.text: A programmer is designing the processes of a new online shop using flowcharts.

parts.title: Symbols
parts.text: Draw a line to link each step to the flowchart symbol used for it.

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–Parallelogram, L2–Rectangle, L3–Diamond, L4–Oval. One mark per line.

parts.title: Rules
parts.text: State **two** rules for drawing a clear flowchart.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): one START and END; flow top to bottom with arrows; decisions have two labelled exits; one step per box; correct symbols; no crossing / dangling lines
scheme.model_answer: 1 Every decision has two exits labelled Yes and No. 2 The flowchart has one START and an END.

parts.title: Counting and totalling
parts.text: Explain the difference between counting and totalling, using the online shop as an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Counting adds 1 per event, e.g. number of orders (1)
- Totalling adds a value, e.g. total cost of the orders (1)
scheme.model_answer: Counting adds 1 for each order to find how many orders there are; totalling adds each order's cost to find the total value.

questions.title: Tracing a flowchart
questions.text:
A flowchart for a gym works as follows:

```text
visits ← 0, total ← 0
repeat 4 times:
    INPUT minutes
    IF minutes >= 60 THEN visits ← visits + 1
    total ← total + minutes
OUTPUT visits, total
```

parts.title: Trace table

parts.title: Loop type
parts.text: Identify the type of loop used and explain how you know.

scheme.mark_scheme: Count-controlled (1); it repeats a fixed number of times — 4 (1)
scheme.model_answer: Count-controlled, because it repeats exactly 4 times.

parts.title: Error
parts.text: A student moves `total ← 0` inside the loop. Explain the effect on the output for the same inputs.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- total is reset every repetition (1)
- so the output total is only the last value, 90 (1)
scheme.model_answer: The total is reset to 0 each time, so at the end it holds only the last value, 90, instead of 265.

questions.title: Library fines
questions.text: *When books are returned, the librarian enters the number of days each book is late. The fine is 100 tenge per day, but never more than 2000 tenge per book. The librarian keeps entering numbers of days; entering **-1** stops the process. Then the total of all fines is displayed.*

parts.title: Draw
parts.text: Draw a flowchart for this process.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- total ← 0 before the loop (1)
- INPUT days (1)
- decision days = -1 to stop / loop condition (1)
- fine ← days × 100 (1)
- decision fine > 2000 (1) → fine ← 2000 (1)
- total ← total + fine and loop back to input (1)
- OUTPUT total then END (1)
scheme.model_answer: START → total ← 0 → INPUT days → days = -1? Yes → OUTPUT total → END; No → fine ← days × 100 → fine > 2000? Yes → fine ← 2000 → total ← total + fine → back to INPUT days

summary: Designing processes with flowcharts — the standard symbols, sequence, selection and iteration, validation processes, counting and totalling loops, tracing a flowchart, converting between flowcharts and pseudocode, and the rules for drawing clear flowcharts.

blocks.content: A diagram that shows the **steps of a process or algorithm in order**, using standard **symbols** joined by **arrows** (flow lines). It shows the **inputs, processing, decisions, loops and outputs** of one process in a system.
In the **design** stage, the DFD shows **what** processes the system has; a **flowchart** shows **how** each process works, step by step, so that a programmer can code it.

blocks.title: Flowchart symbols
rows: A question with **two exits** (Yes / No, True / False)
A procedure or function defined elsewhere
Saving to a database or file

blocks.content:
- **One START** and at least one **END**.
- Flow from **top to bottom** (and left to right); arrows show direction.
- Every **decision** has exactly **two labelled exits** (Yes/No).
- Each box contains **one** clear step.
- Loops return to a point **before** the decision that controls them.
- No arrow ends in mid-air; lines should not cross where avoidable.

blocks.title: Counting and totalling
blocks.content:
- **Counting:** a counter starts at **0** and increases by **1** each time an event happens — `count ← count + 1`.
- **Totalling:** a total starts at **0** and the **value** is added each time — `total ← total + price`.
- Always **initialise** counters and totals **before** the loop.
Many processes in a system **validate input**: they keep asking until the data is acceptable.

flowchart TB
  A([START]) --> B[/INPUT name, gender, email, password/]
  B --> C{"email contains @ and . ?"}
  C -- No --> D[/OUTPUT Invalid e-mail/]
  D --> B
  C -- Yes --> E{"password has an uppercase letter and a digit?"}
  E -- No --> F[/OUTPUT Weak password/]
  F --> B
  E -- Yes --> G[(Save client data in the database)]
  G --> H[/OUTPUT Password accepted/]
  H --> I([END])
blocks.caption: Registration process with validation

blocks.title: Building a validation loop
items: **Decision**: does it meet the rule (range, format, presence)?
**No** → output an **error message** and go **back to the input**.
**Yes** → continue with the next step (store, calculate, output).

blocks.title: Trace the counting flowchart with 4 students (times 8:20, 8:35, 8:31, 8:25; limit 4)

blocks.content:
count ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 850
    INPUT time
    IF time > 8:30 THEN
        count ← count + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT i
OUTPUT count

rows: Diamond + arrow back **up** to before it
`WHILE … ENDWHILE` (test at the top) or `REPEAT … UNTIL` (test at the bottom)

blocks.title: Exam-style mark schemes
blocks.content:
**Q: Draw a flowchart of the Product Price Calculator app using a loop structure. [5]**
Marks for: a **condition** (decision) (1), a **loop** back to repeat (1), **input** (1), **output** (1), a **process** (calculation) (1).

**Q: Create a flowchart for counting late students (850 students, first lesson at 8:30). [4]**
Loop for **850** students (1); **input** each arrival time (1); **decision** `time > 8:30` (1); **count ← count + 1** and output the count after the loop (1).

**Q: Draw a flowchart for the registration process that validates the e-mail (contains "." and "@") and the password (uppercase letters and numbers), stores the data and shows a confirmation. [5]**
Input of the four items (1); e-mail validation decision (1); password validation decision (1); store in the database (1); confirmation message, with invalid data looping back (1).

- Using a rectangle for input/output, or a parallelogram for a calculation.
- Decisions with only **one** exit, or exits not labelled Yes/No.
- Forgetting to **initialise** the counter or total, or initialising it **inside** the loop.
- A loop that never changes its counter — an **infinite loop**.
- Missing START or END.
